'''''Viola palustris''''' ('''marsh violet''' or '''alpine marsh violet''') is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[forb]] of the genus ''[[Viola (plant)|Viola]]''. It inhabits moist meadows, marshes, and stream banks in northern parts of [[North America]] and [[Eurasia]]. The species [[epithet]] ''palustris'' means "marsh-loving".

==Description==
[[File:Viola palustris 6796.JPG|thumb|The lateral petals are lightly bearded. The lobed [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]] is [[Glabrousness|glabrous]].]]
''Viola palustris'' is a [[perennial plant]] that grow to {{Convert|3 to 21.5|cm|sp=us}}.<ref name="Little & McKinney" /> During the summer they often form small colonies connected together by pale [[stolon]]s that root frequently and that are leafy at the [[Node (plants)|nodes]].<ref name="Little">{{cite web |last1=Little |first1=R. John |date=2012 |title=''Viola palustris'' |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=48266 |website=Jepson eFlora |publisher=University of California, Berkeley |access-date=24 June 2025 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250317192959/https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=48266 |archive-date=17 March 2025}}</ref><ref name="Little & McKinney" /> Plants will also have slender and fleshy [[rhizome]]s, modified underground stems.<ref name="Little & McKinney">{{Cite web <!--Deny Citation Bot-->|last1=Little |first1= R. John |last2=McKinney |first2=Landon E. |date=5 November 2020 |orig-date=In print 2015 |url=https://floranorthamerica.org/Viola_palustris |title=''Viola palustris'' |website=[[Flora of North America]] |page=142 |language=en |isbn=978-0-19-534027-3 |oclc=951153367 |access-date=24 June 2025 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250323003917/https://floranorthamerica.org/Viola_palustris |archive-date=23 March 2025}}</ref>

All the leaves are [[basal leaves|basal]], attached to the base of the plant rather than to stems, by hairless [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] that are {{Convert|1 to 17|cm|sp=us|sigfig=2}} long. The leaves do not have lobes, but do have hairless edges that are [[crenulate]], a very fine rounded tooth edge. Their shape varies between [[Reniform leaf|reniform]], [[ovate leaf|ovate]], and [[orbiculate]]; like a kidney with an indentation on the side of the leaf attachment, egg shaped with the wider portion towards the base, and circular in shape. They are 0.5–6.4 cm long and 0.5–5.5 cm wide and more or less as long as wide.<ref name="Little & McKinney" />

The flowers are usually lilac, pale blue, or pale violet on both sides, but are sometimes very pale approaching white.<ref name="Little & McKinney" /> They measure 10 to 13 millimeters across.<ref name="Hitchcock">{{Cite book |last1=Hitchcock |first1=C. Leo |author-link1=Charles Leo Hitchcock |last2=Cronquist |first2=Arthur |author-link2=Arthur Cronquist |date=1977 |orig-date=First printing 1961 |title=Vascular Plants of the Pacific Northwest |url=https://archive.org/details/vascularplantsof0000leoc |url-access=registration |language=en |volume=3: Saxifragaceae to Ericaceae |edition=First |location=Seattle, Washington |publisher=University of Washington Press |page=450 |isbn=978-0-295-73985-4 |oclc=1331012853 |access-date=25 June 2025}}</ref>

The bottom middle petal and sometimes the two petals to either side have violet [[floral guide]]s.<ref name="Little & McKinney" /> The lateral pair are lightly bearded.<ref name="Hitchcock" />

==Taxonomy==
''Viola palustris'' was given its scientific name by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753. It has two accepted [[subspecies]], ''juressi'' and the [[Autonym (botany)|autonym]] ''palustris''. It is part of the genus [[Viola (plant)|''Viola'']] in the family [[Violaceae]].<ref name="POWO" />

The species has {{table row counter|id=Synonyms}} [[Synonym (botany)|synonyms]] of the species or one of its two subspecies.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="POWO subsp. juressi" /><ref name="POWO subsp. palustris" />

===Names===
The species name, ''palustris'', is listed in texts about [[Botanical Latin]] with the meaning "marsh loving".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Smith |first1=Archibald William |title=A Gardener's Book of Plant Names: A Handbook of the Meaning and Origins of Plant Names |date=1963 |publisher=Harper & Row |location=New York |edition=First |page=270 |oclc=710612 |url=https://archive.org/details/gardenersbookofp00smit |access-date=24 June 2025 |language=en}}</ref> It is known by the [[common name]]s ''marsh violet'' or ''alpine marsh violet''.<ref name="NRCS">{{Cite usda plants |symbol=VIPA4 |title=Viola palustris |date=24 June 2025}}</ref><ref name="VASCAN">{{Cite web |last1=Acadia University |last2=Université de Montréal Biodiversity Centre |last3=University of Toronto Mississauga |last4=University of British Columbia |date=2025 |title=''Viola palustris'' Linnaeus - Database of Vascular Plants of Canada (VASCAN) |url=https://data.canadensys.net/vascan/taxon/9503?lang=en |website=Canadensys |language=en |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206213442/https://data.canadensys.net/vascan/taxon/9503?lang=en |archive-date=6 December 2021 |access-date=24 June 2025}}</ref> It is also sometimes called the ''northern marsh violet''.<ref name="VASCAN" />

==Range and habitat==
Marsh violets are native to Europe and North America as well as a small area in northern Africa and a portion of western Asia. In Asia it grows just in [[Western Siberia]] in Russia. To the east in Europe it is native to almost every country, but is absent from southern Russia, [[Crimea]] in Ukraine, [[European Turkey]], Albania, the islands of [[Sicily]], [[Sardinia]], the archipelago of [[Svalbard]], and the [[Balearic Islands]]. It is recorded as locally extinct in [[Hungary]]. They are found in the [[Azores]] in the Atlantic Ocean.<ref name="POWO" />

In north America their range includes Greenland and most of Canada except for the [[Yukon]], Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island.<ref name="POWO" /> In the western United States it grows in mountainous areas of Washington, Oregon, northern coastal California, Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming. It also grows in parts of Nevada and Utah and is reported without specific locations in Arizona, Colorado, and South Dakota. It also has been recorded by the Natural Resources Conservation Service as native to the northeastern states of New York, Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine.<ref name="NRCS" />

Marsh violets grow in marshes, fens, swamps, wet forests, and along stream banks. They grow at sea level all the way to {{Convert|1800|m|sp=us}} in elevation.<ref name="Little & McKinney" />

==Ecology==
It is used as a larval foodplant by the [[pearl-bordered fritillary]] (''Boloria euphrosyne'') and the [[small pearl-bordered fritillary]] (''Boloria selene''), though the small pearl-bordered fritillary prefers the marsh violet and the pearl-bordered fritillary prefers [[common dog-violet]] (''Viola riviniana''). It is also used as a host plant by the [[dark green fritillary]] (''Speyeria aglaja'').<ref>{{cite book |last1=Porter |first1=Keith |last2=Steel |first2=Caroline A. |last3=Thomas |first3=Jeremy A. |author3-link=Jeremy A. Thomas |editor1-last=Dennis |editor1-first=Roger L.H. |title=The Ecology of Butterflies in Britain |date=1992 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford; New York |isbn=978-0-19-854025-0 |pages=143, 278 |url=https://archive.org/details/ecologyofbutterf0000unse_m2f2 |url-access=registration |access-date=25 June 2025 |chapter=7: Butterflies and communities}}</ref> It is a known host for ''[[Hendersonia violae]]'' and ''[[Puccinia fergussonii]]'', two [[pathogenic fungi]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hallgrímsson |first1=Helgi |last2=Eyjólfsdóttir |first2=Guðríður Gyða |date=2004 |title=Íslenskt sveppatal I - smásveppir |url=https://rafhladan.is/bitstream/handle/10802/4090/Fjolrit_45.pdf?sequence=1 |trans-title=Checklist of Icelandic Fungi I - Microfungi |journal=Fjölrit Náttúrufræðistofnunar |language=is, en |volume=45 |publisher=Náttúrufræðistofnun Íslands [Icelandic Institute of Natural History] |page=151 |access-date=24 June 2025}}</ref>
